::: {.section-card}
### NLP Processing Methods

This annex documents the natural-language-processing steps behind the
skills measures used in the report. The main Methodology section shows the
six-step pipeline; this annex explains what happens inside those steps and
why the choices matter for interpretation.
:::

::: {.section-card}
### Step 01 — Language Detection {#pipeline-step-01}

Most Pracuj.pl postings are in Polish, but a non-trivial share contains
English titles, English descriptions, or mixed-language text. We detect the
language of both the title and the full description so that Polish text can
pass through unchanged while non-Polish fields are routed to translation.

Language detection is applied per field rather than per posting because a
common online-vacancy pattern is an English title with a Polish body, or the
reverse. This avoids translating already-usable Polish text and keeps the
downstream corpus consistent.
:::

::: {.section-card}
### Step 02 — Translation {#pipeline-step-02}

All downstream extraction is run on a harmonised Polish text field. Postings
already detected as Polish are kept unchanged; English and other-language
fields are translated into Polish using Gemma 3 Translate 4B. Both original
and translated fields are retained so that analysts can inspect source text
when reviewing specific matches.

This step is needed because the same skill can otherwise appear in several
languages within one analytical sample. Translation makes skill extraction,
job-title standardisation, and taxonomy matching operate on a common-language
input rather than mixing Polish, English, and hybrid phrasing.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Translation routing"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 40, 'rankSpacing': 50}} }%%
flowchart LR
    A["Raw posting"] --> B{"Language<br/>detected?"}
    B -->|"Already Polish"| C["Keep original text"]
    B -->|"English / other"| D["Gemma 3 Translate 4B"]
    D -->|"title + description"| E["Translated Polish text"]
    C --> F["Unified Polish corpus"]
    E --> F
```
:::

::: {.section-card}
### Step 03 — Skill-Sentence Filtering {#pipeline-step-03}

Job descriptions contain many sentences that are not skill requirements:
benefits, company history, application instructions, equal-opportunity
statements, and legal clauses. Before mapping to skills, we isolate the
sentences that actually describe required competences, tasks, tools, or
knowledge.

We use a fine-tuned BERT-style sentence classifier based on the SkillLess
approach. Each sentence is labelled as skill-relevant or non-skill. In this
sample, roughly 40–60% of description text is filtered out before semantic
matching. This improves precision because the ESCO matcher only sees
sentences that plausibly contain skills.
:::

::: {.section-card}
### Step 04 — ESCO Skill Mapping {#pipeline-step-04}

Skill-relevant sentences are mapped to the European Skills, Competences,
Qualifications and Occupations taxonomy (ESCO), which contains roughly
13,000 standardised skill and competence entries. ESCO provides the common
language that makes job postings and BUR training descriptions comparable.

The matching model is a custom contrastive bi-encoder. It places job-ad
sentences and ESCO skill labels in a shared embedding space: semantically
matching pairs are pulled closer together, while non-matching pairs are
pushed apart. For example, a sentence such as *experience with SQL and data
visualisation* should be close to ESCO entries such as *use query languages*
and *manage databases*, but far from unrelated labels such as *negotiate
contracts*.

Hard negatives are central to training. The model must distinguish nearby
but incorrect skills, such as *use programming languages* versus *use query
languages*, not only obviously unrelated concepts. This makes the model
better suited to real vacancy text, where employers describe skills in
informal, overlapping, and sometimes ambiguous ways.


Candidate skills are ranked by cosine similarity. A calibrated similarity
threshold is then applied to remove low-confidence matches and control the
number of skills assigned to each posting or training description. The
threshold is tuned on held-out benchmark data to balance precision and
recall.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Skill-to-ESCO matching pipeline"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 50, 'rankSpacing': 55}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}} }%%
flowchart TD
    A["Skill-relevant sentences"] -->|"encode"| B["Contrastive bi-encoder"]
    B -->|"768-d vector"| C["Sentence embedding"]

    D[("ESCO skill catalogue<br/>~13 000 entries")] -->|"pre-computed<br/>768-d vectors"| E["Reference embedding matrix"]

    C --> F{"Cosine similarity ranking"}
    E --> F

    F -->|"top-k candidates"| G["Candidate ESCO skills<br/>with similarity scores"]
    G -->|"score ≥ calibrated threshold"| I["Final matched ESCO skills"]
```

:::

::: {.section-card}
### Step 05 — Job-Title Standardisation {#pipeline-step-05}

Raw job titles are highly variable. The same role can appear as
*Inżynier oprogramowania*, *Backend Developer*, *Programista*,
*Full-Stack Developer*, or *Senior Software Engineer*. To support
occupational analysis, titles are standardised to ESCO occupations.

Titles are first cleaned by removing common noise such as embedded
locations, salaries, and seniority prefixes. Cleaned titles are embedded
with a labour-market language model and matched to a pre-computed index of
ESCO occupation labels using nearest-neighbour search. The best matching
occupation and its similarity score are retained for downstream analysis and
quality filtering.

Where a title is ambiguous, extracted skill context helps interpretation:
two postings with the same generic title can map differently if their skill
profiles imply different occupations.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "Job title standardisation"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 50, 'rankSpacing': 55}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}} }%%
flowchart TD
    A["Translated job title"] --> B["Title cleaning<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>(remove locations, salaries, prefixes)</i>"]
    B -->|"cleaned text"| C["JobBERT-v3 encoder"]
    C -->|"768-d vector"| D["Title embedding"]

    D -->|"query"| F{"FAISS nearest-neighbour search"}

    E[("ESCO occupation index<br/>~3 000 occupations<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>pre-computed 768-d vectors</i>")] -->|"index"| F

    F -->|"best match + cosine score"| G["Standardised ESCO occupation"]
```

:::

::: {.section-card}
### Step 06 — Sector Classification (ISIC/NACE) {#pipeline-step-06}

Sector analysis requires assigning postings to an economic activity. The
pipeline maps standardised ESCO occupations to ISIC/NACE activity codes using
the official ESCO-to-NACE crosswalk. At the two-digit division level used in
this report, NACE Rev. 2.1 and ISIC Rev. 5 share the same division codes and
boundaries, so results are directly comparable across the two systems.

The assignment uses three tiers. If an occupation maps to a single code, the
assignment is deterministic. If all candidate codes share the same two-digit
division, that division is assigned directly. If candidates span several
divisions, the job title and description are compared with candidate sector
labels using multilingual sentence embeddings, and the highest-scoring
candidate is selected. A confidence margin is retained for auditing.

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "ISIC/NACE sector classification"
%%{init: {'flowchart': {'htmlLabels': true, 'nodeSpacing': 30, 'rankSpacing': 45, 'curve': 'basis'}, 'themeVariables': {'fontSize': '13px'}} }%%
flowchart LR
    A["ESCO occupation<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>from Step 05</i>"]
      -->|"look up"| B[("ESCO → ISIC/NACE crosswalk<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>official mapping table</i>")]
    B --> C{"Number of candidate<br/>ISIC/NACE codes?"}

    C -->|"exactly 1"| D["Deterministic<br/>assignment"]
    C -->|"≥ 2, same 2-digit code"| E["Assign shared<br/>ISIC/NACE division"]
    C -->|"≥ 2, different divisions"| F["Embedding-based disambiguation<br/><i style='font-size:0.8em;color:#64748b'>encode job text + each candidate ISIC/NACE label</i>"]

    F -->|"384-d vectors"| H{"Cosine similarity<br/>comparison"}
    H -->|"highest score"| I["Assigned ISIC/NACE code<br/>+ confidence margin"]

    D --> J["Final sector label"]
    E --> J
    I --> J

    classDef step fill:#eef4fb,stroke:#1d4e89,stroke-width:1px,color:#15314B;
    classDef data fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#b45309,stroke-width:1px,color:#7c2d12;
    classDef out  fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#166534,stroke-width:1px,color:#14532d;
    class A,D,E,F,I step;
    class B data;
    class C,H step;
    class J out;
```

:::

::: {.section-card}
### Validation and Benchmarking

The ESCO skill-matching component is benchmarked against the HOUSE and TECH
datasets used in recent ESCO skill-extraction research
(<span class="paper-ref" data-tooltip="Decorte, J. J., Van Hautte, J., Develder, C., and Demeester, T. 2025. Efficient Text Encoders for Labor Market Analysis. IEEE Access."><a class="paper-link" href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11079977/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Decorte et al. (2025)</a></span>).
These datasets contain job postings annotated with gold-standard ESCO skill
labels by human experts. Against these benchmarks, the pipeline improves
reported RP@5 performance by roughly three percentage points relative to the
current state of the art.

The benchmark is not a guarantee that every individual match is correct.
Rather, it supports the use of the extracted skills for aggregate
composition analysis: sectoral shares, regional shares, demand-supply
mismatch, and robustness checks.
:::
